Through the internet we have both an unprecedented access to information and an unprecedented ability to have our existing biases confirmed. I'm not certain which one is winning.

Most people seek out like minded individuals. I think the bias confirmation is clearly winning.

It is a little scary, as it makes people feel validation and support for some really weird shit that you normally wouldnt find anyone in real life to agree with you on.
confirmation bias by a LONG shot. Not even on the same graph. Most people don't want to look at both sides and be truly neutral. All of us included at one time or another.

The same has been true of every new communication medium in history. Things are just faster this time.

That's not to say we should sit idle. The internet needs further democratization and hardening in the form of decentralization and builtin encryption. Web is cool, but we can do better.

Soon we'll have virtual worlds overlayed atop of the physical one. Going from one reality to the next will be like flipping through TV channels. Not only will people live in a bubble on the net, but in the real world too.

In my opinion information is probably winning.

The thing that's really changed for the confirmation bias side is that they've become more cocksure than ever because now you can go find thousands of authoritative sounding web pages that agree with just about any view no matter how absurd. And the echo chambers further reinforce this cocksuredness. Add social media into the picture and they sound louder than ever, but I think it's not because there's more of them than ever but because they've been given a megaphone and confidence boost.

I think one of the most recent pieces of evidence in favor of information gain is this election. The lengths the media and corporations were going to try to force Hillary into office was completely unprecedented -------- and it didn't work. Democratic turnout was lower than it's been in 20 years and she lost because the people decided, for themselves, that she was not fit for the presidency. Whether one agrees with this decision or not is irrelevant. The point is that people are clearly using the internet not just to reinforce their preexisting views but to adapt and change as conditions merit. Since this is clearly true in politics, which is borderline religious in terms of personal bias, I've no doubt this is extremely true in general.
